key_points: B. K. Desai's "End Of An Illusion" blames Khrushchev's manufactured outrage over the U-2 incident for wrecking the May 1960 Paris summit, arguing that Soviet "peaceful coexistence" rhetoric was illusory from the start.
An unsigned item, "Nazis In Office In East Germany", turns Western de-Nazification criticism back on East Germany by cataloguing former Nazi officials serving in its government and judiciary.

The Notes section surveys Indian domestic politics: a Communist by-election win in Calcutta, strain within the Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti as the P.S.P. weighs quitting it, the newly signed Indo-U.S. 17-million-ton foodgrains agreement, and the Punjab government's detention of Akali leader Master Tara Singh.

A correspondent's report on the Maharashtra Seminar covers a mid-May 1960 Bombay gathering on the new state's problems, addressed by Chief Minister Y. B. Chavan, Justice P. B. Gajendragadkar, and Dr. C. D. Deshmukh.

Gabriel Gersh's "Universities Behind The Iron Curtain" describes the Sovietisation of East German universities through class-based admission quotas, compulsory Marxist-Leninist curricula, and a network of missing or imprisoned students and professors.
An unsigned piece, "A Tribute To Stalin!", reproduced from The Economist, reads Alexander Tvardovsky's Pravda poem "So It Was" as a veiled literary indictment of Stalin's cult of personality.
"A Message From Berlin" reprints a West German solidarity statement, signed by figures including Willy Brandt, on the plight of East Berlin under Soviet occupation.

The closing "With Many Voices" column compiles Indian and international press quotations on the Paris summit's collapse and closes with London Times statistics on the proportion of Soviet officials executed since 1917.
V. B. Karnik's "The Saint And The Police" defends Vinoba Bhave's non-violent mission among the Chambal dacoits against Madhya Pradesh police criticism, arguing the two approaches are complementary.

Unsigned Notes cover a hopeful turn in Algeria's war for independence, continued Chinese military consolidation and Tibetan resistance near the Indo-Nepalese border, and Communist Party opportunism in backing the Akali Dal's Punjabi Suba demand.

Adam Adil's "The Lesson Of Turkey" reads the May 1960 military overthrow of Adnan Menderes, alongside Syngman Rhee's fall in Korea, as proof that Asian peoples will no longer tolerate corrupt authoritarian rule.

D. G. Nadkarni's tribute to Boris Pasternak situates him as the last of a vanished generation of European liberal-humanist writers and reads Doctor Zhivago as a protest against regimentation rather than anti-Soviet propaganda.
An unsigned, contributed piece recounts the 1952 kidnapping and 1953 death in Soviet custody of West Berlin jurist Dr. Walter Linse of the Free Jurists' Committee.
M. A. Sreenivasan's "The Three Techniques" attacks the Congress government's Third Five Year Plan as ruling through sedation, confusion, and distraction rather than serving the people.
An unsigned feature marks the tenth anniversary of the Congress for Cultural Freedom, reproducing anniversary messages from Jayaprakash Narayan, Hugh Gaitskell, George Kennan, and C. Rajagopalachari.
The closing "With Many Voices" column gathers press quotations on Khrushchev, the Paris summit, and decolonisation.

V. B. Karnik's "A Leap In The Dark" judges the July 1960 all-India Central Government employees' strike ill-conceived, blaming P.S.P. leaders S. M. Joshi, Nath Pai, and Peter Alvares for rejecting a reasonable government offer.

C. L. Gheevala's "Reflections On The Third Five Year Plan" criticises the draft Plan's bias toward heavy industry, its vague resource-mobilisation assumptions, and its expansion of the public sector as a threat to democratic freedom.

T. R. Fyvel's "Cultural Freedom In Berlin" reports on the Congress for Cultural Freedom's largest-ever Berlin gathering, with sessions led by Raymond Aron and Edward Shils attended by Jayaprakash Narayan and J. K. Galbraith.
An unsigned "Sino-Soviet Differences" piece traces the widening rift between Khrushchev's doctrine of peaceful coexistence and China's insistence that war remains inevitable under imperialism.
M. Devadas Kini reviews Issac Don Levine's "The Mind of an Assassin", on Ramon Mercader's 1940 assassination of Trotsky, framing Mercader as an indifferent "philosophical executioner."
Phiroze J. Shroff reviews S. R. Patel's "Recognition in the Law of Nations", commending its treatment of the Declaratory and Constitutive theories of international recognition.
"With Many Voices" compiles press quotations, including Nehru's expressed belief in Soviet devotion to peace and D. D. Kosambi's criticism of India's solar-cooker research programme.

The unsigned editorial "At The Post" marks the journal's hundredth issue, restating its founding mission against totalitarianism and warning that rapid industrialisation risks pushing India toward the Soviet model.
J. B. H. Wadia's "Thoughts On Education" defends the Indian film industry against Vinoba Bhave's blanket charge that it corrupts youth, calling for informed rather than reflexive criticism.

Philip Spratt's "World Communism Today" argues forty years of Soviet experience have disproved communism's claim to have solved humanity's problems, contrasting Russian diplomatic tactics with Chinese revolutionary action.

Edward Shils's "India: Traditional Past & Western Future" examines the malaise of India's modern intellectual class, torn between charismatic Indian tradition and imported Western rationalism and socialism.

M. R. Masani's "Conflict Of Principles" analyses the 1960 employees' strike as a clash between the right to strike and the need for essential services, recommending compulsory arbitration over an outright ban.

S. R. Mohan Das's "Crisis In Trade Union Movement" faults both government and union leadership for blurring the line between the strike as economic action and political challenge, exposing organisational weakness.
Devadas Kini's "End Of A Dogma" argues trade unions and social legislation have already civilised capitalism into a welfare-oriented "People's Capitalism" without requiring nationalisation.

"Aristide"'s "Effects Of Socialism" documents a growing "Perquisitive Society" of ministerial privilege, citing Defence Minister Krishna Menon's costly Calicut visit, alongside a three-fold attack on free enterprise.

Anand Mohan's "Prospect For Party Government In India" argues Congress's dominance rests on charisma rather than pluralist conviction, framing the new Swatantra Party as the first genuine challenger through the party system.

K. K. Sinha's "Linguistic Frenzy Or Bharatiyata?" responds to the Assam disturbances by calling for a deliberate, merit-based Bharatiyata to counter linguistic parochialism, while Adam Adil's "Soviet Union And Islam" documents the suppression of Islamic institutions in Soviet Central Asia.
M. R. Masani's "Ways And Ways Of Planning" attacks Nehru's Third Plan for concentrating economic and political power in the state, warning it removes all checks on authority.
S. V. Raju's "Chaos In Congo" attributes the Congo's post-independence collapse to entrenched tribalism and Belgian unpreparedness, contrasting it with Ghana's comparatively stable transition.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "A New Course For The Third Plan" uses Imre Nagy's critique of Stalinist Hungarian planning to argue India's Plan repeats the same over-industrialisation errors.
Jayaprakash Narayan's "India And Tibet," writing as President of the Afro-Asian Council, argues Tibet's 1950 annexation was coercive and urges India to back Tibetan self-determination at the UN.
An unsigned contributed piece marks the twentieth anniversary of the Soviet annexation of the Baltic states, tracing the Molotov-Ribbentrop protocols and subsequent mass deportations.
M. Devadas Kini reviews Hawthorne Daniel's "The Ordeal of the Captive Nations", describing the Soviet pattern of staged coalition governments used to absorb Eastern Europe.
"With Many Voices" compiles press quotations on the UN General Assembly session, the Congo crisis, and Indian economic policy.

B. K. Desai's "Failure At The U.N." judges the 15th UN General Assembly session a failure, blaming Khrushchev's propaganda tactics while also criticising Nehru's and Krishna Menon's asymmetric treatment of Soviet versus Western conduct.

Unsigned Notes cover French intellectuals' defence of Algerian-war conscripts, Ceylon's proposed press nationalisation, calls to restructure the UN, scepticism toward Moscow's new "Friendship University," and Nehru's dismissive remark to the Times of India.
An open letter from three African students in Moscow (Andrew Amar, Theophilius Okonkwo, Michael Ayih) catalogues racial discrimination and harassment faced by African students in the Soviet Union.

V. B. Karnik reviews Constantine FitzGibbon's novel "When The Kissing Had To Stop", reading its fictional communist takeover of Britain as an explicit warning about India's weaker institutional defences.

"Aristides"'s "Free Enterprise And Democracy" argues Indian private enterprise has met its Plan investment targets despite socialist strictures and should embrace the Forum of Free Enterprise's 1957 Code of Conduct.
An open letter to Khrushchev signed by American intellectuals including Sidney Hook and Daniel Bell presses him to reconcile his UN advocacy for Chinese admission with Chinese Communist bellicosity.
"With Many Voices" collects press quotations critical of Khrushchev's UN conduct and of Nehru's and Krishna Menon's perceived leniency toward Soviet and Chinese communism.
V. B. Karnik's editorial "Our Non-Alignment" argues India's non-alignment collapses repeatedly into de facto alignment with the communist bloc, citing silence on Soviet and Chinese colonialism.

Unsigned Notes survey Algeria's decisive war phase, India's partisan tilt toward Lumumba in the Congo crisis, UNESCO's selective racism coverage, mass arrests during the Punjabi Suba agitation, and the Mauritania-Morocco dispute.
M. R. Masani's "Contributions To Political Funds" argues against corporate political donations as economically distortive and effectively coerced under a licence-permit economy.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "Prime Minister's Marxist Dogmas" contends Nehru's Five Year Plans and cooperative-farming programme are Marxist in substance despite his denials.
An interview with expelled African student S. Omor Okullo, reprinted from U.S. News & World Report, recounts racial discrimination against African students at Moscow University.
M. Devadas Kini reviews two books on Hungarian writers under communism, tracing the arc from Stalinist orthodoxy through the 1956 Revolution.
The closing "With Many Voices" press digest criticises Nehru's handling of Chinese incursions into Ladakh as understating the threat.
V. B. Karnik's "The Party or the People?" uses the Uttar Pradesh Congress crisis over Dr. Sampurnanand's removal to argue that elected representatives must take precedence over party officials.
An unsigned tribute to Ellen Roy, wife and collaborator of M. N. Roy, follows her murder in Dehra Dun and recounts her decades sustaining Radical Humanism.

Notes cover the poorly attended Afro-Asian Solidarity Conference as communist-front propaganda, the Ex-Communists' Convention in Kerala inaugurated by Stephen Spender, and the dissolution of Kashmir's Democratic National Conference.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "Towards A New Liberalism" sets out a "positive liberalism," drawing on T. H. Green and Aristotle, that regulates economic activity for the common good without state ownership.
Aziz Madni's "Whither Cuba?" traces the Cuban revolution's drift from anti-Batista liberation into a new, Soviet-aligned tyranny under Castro, urging U.S. reapproachment.
A contributed piece analyses the December 1960 Moscow Conference of 81 communist parties as an unstable compromise masking real Sino-Soviet rivalry for leadership.
"Democracy—U.P. Style" narrates the internal Uttar Pradesh Congress power struggle in sardonic detail, closing with the installation of Mr. C. B. Gupta as Chief Minister.
"With Many Voices" closes with quotations on neutrality and India's drift toward the Soviet camp.

V. B. Karnik's "A Lesson For Us" argues China's 1959-60 famine exposes the structural failure of communist planning's overemphasis on heavy industry, and warns India's Third Plan risks the same mistake.
S. R. Mohan Das's "Bhavnagar Congress Convention" dissects Nehru's dominance over the 66th Congress session's resolutions and the "ginger group's" defeat in party elections.

Notes cover uncovered Soviet espionage rings in India, the French referendum strengthening de Gaulle's hand on Algeria, the arrest of Olga Ivinskaya, Milovan Djilas's conditional release, and rival Brazzaville/Casablanca blocs in Africa.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "Towards Party-less Democracy" expounds M. N. Roy's and Jayaprakash Narayan's proposal for a partyless parliamentary system built on polling-booth voters' associations.

An unsigned contributed piece, "Soviet Economic Growth & the West," compares Soviet and Western growth rates, housing, and living standards, concluding Soviet GNP will remain roughly half that of the U.S. even by 1975.
"The Moscow Soap Opera," reprinted from the Public Relations Journal, argues Khrushchev's folksy theatrics are calculated propaganda technique rather than genuine emotion.
B. K. Desai reviews a National Review symposium concluding Sino-Soviet differences are tactical rather than a fundamental rift, with China remaining a Russian satellite for the near term.
"Saadi" reviews S. R. Patel's "Foreign Policy of India", which argues Indian foreign policy is "a one-man show" under Nehru driven by a dangerous "obsession with peace."
B. K. Desai's "The Report & After" argues the joint India-China officials' report vindicates India's border claims and calls for India to abandon its wavering non-aligned posture.
Notes call Lumumba's murder a "crime against humanity," criticise the CPI's evasive resolution on Chinese aggression, address the Jabalpur communal riots, and mourn Sol Levitas of The New Leader.
Jayaprakash Narayan's essay on Panchayati Raj argues the institution should become the foundation of "participating democracy," urging genuine devolution and non-partisan village elections.
M. A. Venkata Rao expounds J. K. Galbraith's "The Affluent Society," focusing on the imbalance between private affluence and public squalor and the case for a mixed economy.

S. R. Mohan Das's "Some Reiterations In Democracy" contrasts Britain's organically evolved, non-doctrinaire democracy with India's synthetic, a priori idealism, drawing on Lord Morrison's Bombay lectures.
The Review section covers R. P. Masani's "Britain In India" and A. K. Mukerji and Ram Singh's "Germany Today."
"With Many Voices" compiles quotations on Panchsheel, the China border dispute, Tibet, and shrinking individual liberty.
"A. Democrat"'s "Communists and Democracy" uses Czechoslovakia's coalition-entryism takeover as a warning that Indian communists' parliamentary moderation is tactical, not sincere.
P. V. Thampy's "Without Comment" piece criticises Congress leaders, including Nehru, for lending prestige to the communist-controlled Kerala People's Arts Club.

M. R. Masani's "Choice Before The Country" frames the 1961-62 Budget debate as a choice between a State-directed economy and "real economic democracy" based on market choice, criticising new excise duties and prestige spending.
"Economicus" offers a technical review of the Central Budget 1961-62, defending the tax structure while criticising the blanket cut in development rebate.
A contributed piece surveys deepening famine conditions in China, detailing emergency grain imports, drastically cut rice rations, and hunger riots.
"Saadi"'s "The Place of Muslims In India" traces Muslim frustration to loss of political power under British rule and post-Partition leaderlessness, calling for economic inclusion.
V. B. Karnik reviews Selig Harrison's "India: The Most Dangerous Decades," crediting its warnings on regionalism while faulting it for underweighting India's unifying factors.
"With Many Voices" closes with quotations on communism, the Cold War, and Indian politics.
V. B. Karnik's "Revolt In Cuba" argues the failed anti-Castro revolt was led by genuine disillusioned patriots, not a US-organised invasion as Indian commentary suggested.
"Saadi"'s "Communism Versus Communalism" argues communism, not communalism, is India's greater long-term threat, since it can infiltrate mainstream parties undetected.
Notes cover the collapse of the French generals' revolt in Algeria and Parliament's new Criminal Law Amendment Bill against subversive propaganda.
An unsigned "Without Comment" digest covers the World Peace Council's Delhi conference, where Chinese delegates clashed with Indian hosts over Tibet.
A. K. Menon's "The Defence Debate" reports Acharya Kripalani's charge that Krishna Menon built cliques undermining army morale, linking this to General Thimayya's earlier resignation.
S. R. Mohan Das's "The Sixth Congress of Indian Communists" argues Indian press coverage of the CPI's Vijayawada Congress misreads its underlying unity behind a Moscow-approved line.
Rita Hinden's "The Odds Against Democracy" engages Seymour Lipset's thesis that economic development is a precondition for democracy, citing India as a counter-example.
A review of the International Commission of Jurists' report "South Africa and the Rule of Law" catalogues apartheid's breaches of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

Adam Adil's "Choice Before the Congress" warns that a manufactured Left-Right split within Congress is being exploited by the CPI's strategy of forming a "united front" to capture the party from within.
P. Spratt's "Communist Infiltration Tactics" surveys communist expansion through infiltration of nationalist movements, warning a similar method may already be in progress at India's borders.

An unsigned piece traces six years of communist subversion in South Vietnam following the 1954 Geneva partition, describing Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh disguising its communist core behind nationalist framing.
"A Democrat"'s "The Tragedy of Laos" describes two-thirds of Laos under Pathet Lao control despite U.S. aid and SEATO guarantees.
S. P. Aiyar's "Prospects of Democracy in India" credits British constitutional gradualism and Nehru's temperament for India's democratic stability while flagging weak parliamentary oversight.
The "Without Comment" digest reprints press clippings on Soviet livestock deaths, Communist Party defections to Congress in Punjab, and Moscow Radio's criticism of Nehru's Cuba stance.
M. Devadas Kini reviews S. Chandrasekhar's "Communist China Today" on the communisation of land, labour, and family life under Mao's communes.
"V B. K." reviews Khasa Subba Rau's "Sidelights on Rajaji," framing Rajaji's dissent from Congress as having grown into the Swatantra Party.
S. Sharangpani's lead article calls for India's fragmented opposition parties to unite into a "National Democratic Opposition" bloc against a creeping Congress-Communist alliance.

Oskar Helmer's essay argues Austria's 1955 declaration of neutrality was in substance an enforced neutralisation extracted under Soviet pressure, warning against its drift into "ideological neutralism."

Notes report a British "Prisoners of Conscience" campaign, G. D. Birla's advocacy of expanded Indo-Soviet trade, the Punjab government's arrests of Akali leaders, and the death of journalist Khasa Subba Rau.
K. K. Sinha's report on a Delhi "nationalist Muslim" convention argues real remedies for minority grievances lie in fair administrative practice rather than conferences.
James Burnham's "Laos And Containment" argues Western containment doctrine is structurally bankrupt because it cannot combine halting communist advance with renouncing offensive operations.
Nissim Ezekiel's essay dissects a Bombay magistrate's judgment banning "Lady Chatterley's Lover" as a failure of commonsense rather than merely a threat to free expression.
A "Without Comment" digest tracks the widening Soviet-UAR rift over the treatment of Arab communists.
"With Many Voices" closes with Cold War quotations from Kennedy and Khrushchev, and A. D. Gorwala's satire on the elastic Indian use of "leftist."
Adam Adil's "Berlin Crisis And Western Stand" argues the Western allies must meet Khrushchev's renewed threat to sign a separate East German peace treaty with firm resolve, not concession.

A Nigerian student's first-hand account (Anthony Okotcha) describes Soviet indoctrination and paramilitary subversion training at Moscow's Friendship University aimed at Africa, including a blueprint for assassination-based seizure of power in Nigeria.
V.B.K. reviews Takdir Alisjahbana's "Indonesia In The Modern World," on whether Indonesian nationalism can be redirected from destructive hatred into constructive nation-building.

M. Devadas Kini's "Plans And The Common Man" argues a decade of Indian planning has left ordinary living standards no better off, citing heavy deficit financing and high combined income-and-dividend taxation.

Shorter items cover the 1961 Maharashtra floods and Panshet dam breach, the France-Tunisia Bizerta crisis, India-Pakistan tension over Kashmir, and a British trade-union case exposing Communist ballot-rigging.
"With Many Voices" closes with quotations from Kennedy, Khrushchev, and Chinese Foreign Minister Chen Yi on Berlin and Sino-Soviet relations.
V. B. Karnik's "A Pie In The Sky" dissects the new Soviet Communist Party draft programme as propagandistic utopianism promising abundance by 1980 while reaffirming one-party dictatorship.
Notes cover the Blitz tabloid's parliamentary censure for its attack on Acharya Kripalani and welcome Jomo Kenyatta's release in Kenya.
M. A. Venkata Rao's essay contrasts Auguste Comte's "Religion of Humanity" with Marx's class-war dialectic, proposing humanist associations to widen Indian national sympathy beyond caste and creed.
M. R. Masani's "Planning For Poverty Or Plenty?" attacks the Third Five Year Plan as pursuing Soviet-style "State Capitalism," predicting inflation, unemployment, and threats to fundamental rights.
Willy Brandt's "Warning For East & West," reprinted from The New Leader, warns that a Soviet-East German separate peace treaty would entrench the German border and must not be accepted by the West.
Anand Mohan's "The Neutral Summit" offers a skeptical preview of the Belgrade non-aligned conference, questioning Nasser's leadership credentials and Cuba's genuine neutrality.
A "Without Comment" digest reprints items on German militarisation, Soviet scientists granted asylum, and Cuban students facing execution.

"With Many Voices" includes Kennedy's remark that the source of world trouble is Moscow, not Berlin, alongside a continuation of Karnik's critique of the Soviet draft programme's silence on personal liberty.
Adam Adil's "The Belgrade Conference" argues most delegates at the non-aligned summit were in practice anti-Western, condemning Western colonialism while staying silent on Soviet and Chinese abuses.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "The Mind Of The Electorate" reflects on voter cynicism and caste-based bloc voting drawn from his own Lok Sabha candidacy in Bangalore City, calling for civic education.
An unsigned obituary eulogises UN Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjoeld as a martyr to Congolese unity, killed amid the Congo crisis.

Thomas J. Dodd's "Hungary — The Missed Opportunity" argues the West's failure to act during the 1956 Hungarian Revolution was one of the gravest post-war policy failures, and calls for a "Freedom Academy" to train Free World counteraction.
A report on the Afro-Asian Council's New Delhi meeting, chaired by Jayaprakash Narayan, summarises resolutions on Algeria, Berlin, Tibet, and the Sino-Indian border dispute.

An open letter, "A Reply To Mayor Willy Brandt," signed by intellectuals including Raymond Aron, Jorge Luis Borges, and Sidney Hook, frames the Berlin Wall as a violation of the human right to leave one's country.
Reviews cover Germaine Tillion's "Algeria, the Realities" and C. Rajagopalachari's "Satyam Eva Jayate," the latter framed as building the intellectual case for the Swatantra Party.
A "Without Comment" digest likens Walter Ulbricht's East Germany to Hitler's regime and recounts a farcical cancelled Soviet embassy film screening in London.

An unsigned lead editorial, "Kripalani Vs. Menon," frames the North Bombay parliamentary contest as a referendum on democracy versus communist influence, contrasting Kripalani's Gandhian record with Menon's alleged pro-Soviet sympathies.
Tibor Meray's "The Forgotten People" mourns the fifth anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution and the world's fading attention to continued repression there.
Acharya J. B. Kripalani's own address to North Bombay voters grounds his candidacy in Gandhian principle, criticising Menon's softness toward China and mismanagement of Defence.
S. Sharangpani's "Nasser And Nkrumah" compares the two leaders' pan-nationalist ambitions, tracing the collapse of Nasser's United Arab Republic and Nkrumah's slide into authoritarian rule in Ghana.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Rethinking U.N. Policy In The Congo" argues the UN has neglected Katanga's economic realities and proposes a negotiated settlement with Tshombe rather than destroying his economic order by force.
A "Without Comment" digest reports Communist Party defections to Congress in Warangal and a three-part history of Chinese pressure on India via Tibet and the Sino-Nepalese highway agreement.
"Notes" and "With Many Voices" compile quotations on the North Bombay election, including K. M. Munshi calling Menon a "Trojan Horse" and Kennedy's line on being "neither Red nor dead."

S. Sharangpani's "Non-Alignment Reconsidered" credits Nehru's U.S. visit with repairing damage from Krishna Menon's pro-Soviet UN posturing, especially Nehru's admission that Soviet Eastern Europe involves a form of colonialism.

Adam Adil's "De-Stalinisation Versus Communism" argues Khrushchev's de-Stalinisation is cosmetic, since Stalinism was Leninism's logical extension and can only end by repudiating Marxism-Leninism itself.
G. F. Hudson's "Hitler And Khrushchev" draws an extended parallel between Hitler's pre-war peace rhetoric and Khrushchev's Berlin diplomacy, warning against a repeat of Munich-style capitulation.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "The National Bourgeoisie Under Attack" traces how communist regimes tactically tolerate and then liquidate the "national bourgeoisie," applying the pattern to a 1960 Moscow-directed shift in CPI strategy toward India's own bourgeoisie.

"Nation Against Aggression" compiles Indian editorial excerpts condemning the government's secretive handling of Chinese encroachment in Ladakh and Krishna Menon's double standard toward Goa versus China.
A "Without Comment" miscellany covers chronic Soviet consumer shortages and Warsaw jokes mocking de-Stalinisation.
"With Many Voices" closes with Nehru's remark on Eastern European colonialism and Kennedy's comparison of Soviet versus Western nuclear test megatonnage.

B. K. Desai's "Myth Exposed" defends India's December 1961 military liberation of Goa as the justified end of fourteen years of failed peaceful appeals, arguing it shattered the Western myth of Nehru as a pure apostle of non-violence.

Jayaprakash Narayan's "A Plea For Positive Non-Violent Action" reproduces his statement on Goa, mourning that force was needed while faulting non-violent leaders, himself included, for neglecting active engagement.
P. G. Honey's "Guerrilla War In South Vietnam" traces the Viet Cong insurgency's origins to the 1954 Geneva partition and describes Diem's countermeasures against communist infiltration.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Illusion About Russian Foreign Policy" attacks Nehru's belief that Soviet and Chinese communism are more nationalist than internationalist, citing Stalin's broken postwar promises.
Adam Adil's "United Nations & Congo" questions the legitimacy of UN military force against Katanga's secession, arguing Tshombe enjoys genuine popular support.
A contributed piece on "Communist Conspiracy In Guinea" recounts President Sekou Toure's expulsion of the Soviet ambassador after uncovering an alleged subversive plot.
A "Without Comment" digest and press-clipping cluster note CPI general secretary Ajoy Ghosh's pledge of support for Krishna Menon's candidacy and his contradictory statements on Chinese aggression.

A reader's letter on an Ahmedabad transport strike is offered as a cautionary tale about nationalisation, and "With Many Voices" closes with quotations mocking Nehru's inconsistency on non-violence and force.

Fritz Schatten's "A Lesson From Guinea" narrates Soviet ambassador Solod's 1961 expulsion from Conakry as a diplomatic failure, cataloguing bungled Eastern-bloc aid projects that disillusioned Guineans.
Acharya J. B. Kripalani explains his North Bombay candidacy as a stand against government policy trends associated with Krishna Menon, citing concealment of Chinese border incursions from Parliament.

James Burnham's "On The Horns Of Our Dilemma" argues the West must choose nuclear war or communist conquest as its "main enemy," criticising Kennedy for refusing to choose and thereby producing an incoherent policy.
An unsigned contributed piece surveys China's hardening frontier disputes with India even as it settles boundary agreements favourable to itself with Nepal and Burma.
An unsigned piece, condensed from Le Figaro, indicts Khrushchev's own fulsome praise of Stalin during the 1930s purges and his role in exterminating Ukraine's Communist Party leadership.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "The Mystery Of Nehru's Action On Goa" suspects a communist-aligned "ginger group" pushed Nehru toward force in Goa to rehabilitate Krishna Menon's prestige.
John Rosselli profiles the British magazine Encounter on its hundredth issue, praising its vigour on ideas while diagnosing a "narcissism" about British intellectual society.
A "Without Comment" digest covers Polish private farming, alleged Chinese and Soviet funding of Kenyan politician Oginga Odinga, and West Bengal communists cancelling Stalin Day.

S. N. Aiyer's "Press And The Prime Minister" argues the North Bombay election exposed Nehru's growing intolerance of press criticism, including a Congress-instigated bonfire of the Indian Express and Loksatta.
Melvin J. Lasky's "The Art And Science Of Being Neutral" uses Switzerland's wartime experience under General Henri Guisan to argue genuine neutrality requires costly preparedness, not rhetoric.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Gresham's Law In Politics," written as a Jana Sangh Lok Sabha candidate, reports widespread voter cynicism and argues Swatantra and Jana Sangh are the strongest counterweight to Congress and communist influence.
Jean Bloch-Michel's "The Plastic Bombers" reports on escalating OAS bomb terrorism against French and Algerian journalists and intellectuals favouring a negotiated Algerian peace.
Fritz Schatten's "Young Somalis' Adventures In Prague" recounts six Somali students fleeing Czechoslovakia after surveillance, censorship, and religious discrimination under communist rule.
Ernest Kux's "Cat Among The Peace Pigeons" reports open Sino-Soviet discord at the Stockholm World Peace Council meeting over whether to prioritise disarmament or anti-colonial struggle.
B. K. Desai's lead essay reads the Third General Election as a Congress victory masking organisational decline and a widening space for the Swatantra Party and Jan Sangh.
V. B. Karnik's "North Bombay Election" dissects Krishna Menon's defeat of Kripalani, attributing it to Congress organisational muscle, Nehru's intervention, and Communist mobilisation.

S. R. Mohan Das's "The Resurgence Of The D.M.K." traces the party's lineage from the anti-Brahmin Justice Party to Annadurai's culturally organised DMK, arguing its separatism is tactical rather than core ideology.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "The Elephant, The Mahout And Raja" warns Menon's win signals a CPI strategy of infiltrating Congress from within toward a future "National Unity" coalition.
A contributed piece reports the deepening Sino-Soviet rift, with Peking's support for Albania read as an indirect attack on Khrushchev's "revisionism."
E. P. Whittemore's "Cuba's Unions Come Full Circle" chronicles the Confederation of Cuban Workers' return to complete Communist control, purging genuine anti-Batista labour leader David Salvador.
A "Without Comment" digest reports the arrest of Soviet writer Mikhail Naritza and the suicide of Polish journalist Henryk Holland amid a crackdown on liberal journalists.
"With Many Voices" closes with Krishna Menon denying he needs to prove his patriotism and Nehru affirming that private enterprise is good for India.

K. Sheshadri's "China & Aggression" welcomes the government's refusal to renew the 1954 Panchsheel trade agreement with China until border aggression is vacated, while criticising Krishna Menon's equivocal statements.
Ernest Halperin's "The New Djilas Affair" covers Milovan Djilas's renewed persecution in Yugoslavia over his manuscript "Conversations with Stalin."
Notes discuss China's secretive National People's Congress amid economic hardship and Britain's Radcliffe Report on communist infiltration of Civil Service unions.

A contributed piece, "Asian Reds Between Moscow & Peking," surveys how Asian communist parties are positioning themselves in the Sino-Soviet split, noting the Indian Communist Party's own division following Ajoy Ghosh's death.
Adam Adil's "Ghana - A One-Party State" indicts Nkrumah's use of preventive detention and one-party consolidation as a betrayal of Ghana's democratic promise.
John B. Wood's "Albania's Moves Under Scrutiny" concludes Albania remains too economically dependent on China to turn West despite its quarrel with Moscow.
A "Without Comment" digest covers Czechoslovak and Polish agriculture, halted Russian aid to China, and preparations reportedly underway to rehabilitate Boris Pasternak.
"With Many Voices" includes de Gaulle on the Soviet "totalitarian empire" and a jab that Nehru is "the world's greatest self-contradictor."

V. B. Karnik's lead essay on Panchayati Raj weighs its democratic promise against the risk of capture by monied or casteist local interests, urging consensus-based rather than contested village elections.
Notes welcome Dr. Radhakrishnan's election as President, condemn Djilas's secret trial in Yugoslavia, and question the secrecy surrounding India's reported MIG jet deal with the Soviet Union.

An unsigned report traces troubled preparations for the Communist-organised World Youth Festival planned for Helsinki, describing it as an instrument of international communist policy over Finnish objections.
S. R. Mohan Das's report on the Hind Mazdoor Sabha's Coimbatore convention traces the union federation's decline from nearly 900,000 to roughly 250,000 members since the 1950 Bombay textile strike.
V. B. K. reviews T. H. Tetens's "The New Germany and the Old Nazis", judging its claims about a revived Nazi presence in West Germany likely one-sided but useful for balance.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Revolutionary Defeatism" applies Lenin's doctrine of welcoming one's own government's defeat to warn that Indian Communists would ideologically favour Indian military defeat in a future clash with China.
A "Without Comment" digest covers delayed Soviet generator deliveries, Chinese firing on an Indian policeman at Kalimpong, and rising Soviet executions.
"With Many Voices" closes with Khrushchev mocking "pants-less Communism" and Frank Moraes criticising Nehru's economic thinking as decades out of date.

Adam Adil's "Constructive Path To Disarmament" criticises the Delhi Anti-Nuclear Arms Convention as a de facto propaganda boost to the Soviet side, arguing disarmament without inspection would let the USSR rearm covertly.

Notes address disproportionate outrage over the UN's Kashmir resolution, Kerala's Congress-P.S.P. coalition crisis, India's foreign-travel currency restrictions, and opposition to India acquiring Soviet MIG aircraft.

V. B. Karnik's "Refugees From China" describes roughly 80,000 refugees fleeing into Hong Kong in May 1962, indicting Communist agricultural failure under the Great Leap Forward and the credulity of Western sympathisers like Lord Boyd Orr.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Principles Of National Integration" argues India's independence struggle produced only negative unity against British rule, and criticises Congress for intensifying caste and communal preferential treatment.
A reader's letter, "Who Betrayed Indians In China," recounts the persecution of India's business community in China after 1949 and blames Ambassador K. M. Panikkar's passivity.
N. C. Zamindar's "A Basic Fallacy Of Socialism" argues Marxist materialism wrongly reduces the plurality of human motive to economics alone, citing altruism as counter-evidence.
A "Without Comment" digest reports Cuban labour leader David Salvador's 30-year sentence and Portugal's forced-labour system in Angola.
A review of "Mahatma in the Marxist Mirror" notes communist statements on Gandhi consistently branding him a reactionary friend of capitalists.
K. K. Sinha's "West Bengal Opens A New Chapter" examines the succession after Dr. B. C. Roy's death, mapping the coming rivalry between new Chief Minister P. C. Sen and P.C.C. president Atulya Ghosh.
Raman K. Desai surveys the European Common Market's origins and estimates a net annual loss to India of roughly Rs. 17 crores if Britain joins on the terms then discussed.
Rama Swarup Sabherwal's "Communist Dictatorship In North Korea" describes Kim Il Sung's regime as consolidated through violent internal purges, sham elections, and militarised farm collectivisation.
Adam Adil reports a shift in American education toward teaching about communism in schools, following decades of restriction under laws such as Georgia's "Americanism" statute.
A letter praises Speaker Hukum Singh's even-handed conduct, and Jasha M. Levi's "A Tribute to Djilas" honours the imprisoned Yugoslav dissident's courage in standing trial again.
John S. Connor's "Despirited Economics" rebuts an economist's defence of prohibition, arguing it ignores worker-disincentive effects and squeezes the investable surplus.
M. A. Venkata Rao's essay on Dravidian separatism traces DK/DMK politics to Brahmin-dominance resentment, invoking Jung's collective-neurosis theory and urging sympathetic engagement over force.
"With Many Voices" closes with Clinton Rossiter calling Nehru "cranky, preachy and imperious" and Wilhelm Roepke citing the Berlin Wall as proof of communism's true character.
V. B. Karnik's "The First Step" criticises the government's retreating negotiating position on Chinese aggression in Ladakh and calls for breaking off diplomatic relations with China.
N. C. Zamindar's "Madhya Pradesh Scene" surveys factional Congress infighting and warns the state risks becoming "another Kerala" as communists exploit the disunity.
Margaret Roberts's "Hunger In South Africa" documents severe malnutrition and rising infant mortality among non-white South Africans amid destroyed agricultural surpluses.

M. R. Pai's "Predominance Of The Economic Factor" cites a 0.3 per cent return on state enterprise investment and a Mysore bicycle factory producing 18 bicycles in two and a half years as evidence of political override of economic rationality.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "Dogma Versus Development In Our Plans" attacks the Third Plan's ideological commitment to state monopoly over "commanding heights" industries.
A contributed piece analyses communist opposition, from Moscow, Peking, and local parties, to the proposed Federation of Malaysia.
Wolfgang Leonhard judges the 1962 Helsinki World Youth Festival a failure, citing attendance shortfalls masked by substitute Soviet "delegates" and the absence of free discussion.
Reviews cover Patrick van Rensberg's "Guilty Land" on apartheid and Thomas Hodgkin's "African Political Parties."
B. K. Desai's "Significance Of Berlin" uses the shooting of Peter Fechter at the Wall to argue the West has been too passive against Soviet "salami tactics" in the divided city.
Notes criticise Nehru for treating Soviet expansionism as benign while condemning Chinese aggression, and discuss the Djakarta Asian Games "Sondhi Affair."
A report on the Liberal International's Hague Council meeting reproduces resolutions on the EEC, apartheid South Africa, and a "Freedom For All" declaration rejecting appeasement of communism.
Adam Adil surveys the disarray of pan-Arab politics after the Algeria settlement, noting the fractured Arab League and a hopeful Saudi-Jordanian semi-union.
M. A. Venkata Rao's "Tradition And Socialism" contrasts the pluralist, vocation-based ethics of Indian dharma with Marxism's drive toward an imagined single classless society.
Raman Desai reviews Milovan Djilas's "Conversations with Stalin", recounting Stalin's court atmosphere and Soviet economic bullying of Albania and Yugoslavia.
Aziz Madni reviews Ram Gopal's "The Trials of Nehru", documenting nine trials in which Nehru, defiant, refused to recognise British court legitimacy.
Humphrey Evans's "Trade Unions In China" argues Chinese Communist unions function as instruments of Party control and foreign propaganda rather than worker advocacy.

V. B. Karnik's "Preconditions To Victory" frames the Chinese offensive in Ladakh and NEFA as part of a global communist bid for domination alongside Vietnam, Berlin, and Cuba, and calls for foreign military aid, a broadened government, and the Defence Minister's removal.

Richard Moore's "Winning The Cold War" argues liberals cannot be neutral in the Cold War since totalitarian claims to total authority are inherently in conflict with liberty, and that ideological attack is the best form of defence.
Moore's essay debunks the communist-promoted "myth of neo-colonialism," arguing nationalism in newly independent states works against, not for, communism.

Moore proposes a pragmatic, differentiated liberal stance toward anti-communist but illiberal regimes such as Diem's Vietnam, and calls for a "Great Debate" using open scientific and intellectual exchange as ideological attack.

S. Natarajan reviews Gyula Paloczi-Horvath's biography of Khrushchev, crediting its account of his rise to power through mastery of the party machine and the collectively authored de-Stalinisation speech.

Natarajan's review questions the book's claim of deep popular Soviet disgust with party bureaucracy as overstated, and notes its account of persistent Sino-Soviet tension beneath a maintained "appearance of monolithic unity."

M. R. Masani's "A Democracy At War" accuses the Nehru government of suppressing evidence of Chinese incursions from Parliament since 1954 and surveys the fractured opposition's divergent wartime positions.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "The Iron Curtain And World Peace" frames the Curtain as psychological "mind-control," proposing world federation and mobilised opinion, not unilateral gestures, as the true route to peace.
An unsigned report assesses whether Chiang Kai-shek will exploit the Sino-Indian war to invade the mainland, concluding U.S. treaty restraints make this unlikely despite his readiness.
A short item reports 194 executions in the Soviet Union over twelve months, most for economic crimes, reading it as anxiety over the command economy's inefficiency.
Tunku Abdul Rahman's radio address frames the India-China war as an ideological contest between communism and democracy, announcing a Malayan "Save Democracy Fund" for India.

N. C. Zamindar's "Some Thoughts On Defence" criticises Nehru's claimed modernising credentials given India's ill-equipped army, calling for an ideological defence grounded in Dharma and Gandhian courage.

A review of Donald S. Zagoria's "The Sino-Soviet Conflict 1956-1961" praises its evenhanded account of the widening Moscow-Peking rift, judging Khrushchev's caution favourably against Mao's "revolutionary hubris."
